       Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) 536/2014, Chapter IV

                                                          22
       368.      In case of an urgent safety measure which requires an update of protocol, it is
          expected that the notiﬁcation of the USM is submitted immediately to inform of the
          applied changes and/or planned changes, as of CTR with undue delay but not later than
          7 days from the date the measures have been taken. That USM information must be
          followed by a submission of the documents as SM (substantial amendment for
          approval“.


7.28 Question: What should be the terminology, format
     and standards for SUSAR reporting to EVCTM?
       369.      Use of terminology: For the classiﬁcation, retrieval, presentation,
          evaluation and assessment, electronic exchange and communication of SUSAR
          information to EVCTM, sponsors should apply the terminology as of Article 25 of
          the Implementing Regulation (IR) 520/2012 (amended July 2025)17.

       370.       Use of internationally agreed formats and standards: For the description,
          retrieval, presentation, evaluation and assessment, electronic exchange and
          communication of SUSARs, sponsors should apply the following formats and
          standards as of Article 26 of the IR 520/2012 (amended July 2025).

       371.     The current version of the EU Individual Case Safety Report (ICSR)
          Implementation Guide also see ICH E2B (R3).

       372.      Reference is also made to EMA’s Guidelines on Good Pharmacovigilance
          Practices (GVP), particularly module VI on ‘Collection, management and
          submission of reports of suspected adverse reactions to medicinal products.

       373.       Sponsors shall report SUSARs electronically to the Eudravigilance
          database via EVWEB or using the E2B (R3) electronic ICSR forms. To help sponsors
          with SUSAR reporting, a web-based form was developed in accordance with
          Article 40.2 of the CTR in the Clinical Trials Module of the Eudravigilance database
          (“EVWEB report form”). This form was developed in compliance with Annex III 2.3
          of the CTR and based on international guidance documents (including ICH E2B
          (R3)). The use of this form supports regulatory compliance with EU law and
          harmonisation of safety data, and it incorporates the relevant standards and
          terminology.




 17
      Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 520/2012

                                                  23
      7.29 Question: What is the minimum
      information to be provided in the SUSAR
      reports?
       374.    Answer: The minimum information to be provided for an initial report of a
          SUSAR is deﬁned in Annex III section 2.3. in the CTR.

       375.     There are speciﬁc ﬁelds in individual case safety reports (ICSRs) that must
          be completed for a valid SUSAR submission. These ﬁelds exist to collect the
          necessary data for appropriate safety reporting to ensure trial subject's safety.
          Sponsors shall ensure that SUSAR ICSRs are as complete as possible and shall
          communicate updates of reports to EVCTM timely, accurately and reliably.

       376.      Note data conﬁdentiality is given by masking rules provided in the
          Addendum 2 to GVP Module IV18. Please chose the correct report type, study type,
          including EU CT number (or protocol code if CT only conducted outside EU/EEA),
          and date. The dates refer to the day on which the report was ﬁrst received from the
          source and the date of receipt of the most recent information.

       377.      A case narrative, should be included presenting the information in a logical
          time sequence, in the chronology of the patient’s experience including clinical
          course, therapeutic measures, outcome and follow-up information obtained, as
          well as information of unblinding (date and which treatment the individual subject
          has received; see Question 7.22. A clear statement has to be made on whether
          the SAR is unexpected or not (i.e. included in the RSI or not).

       378.     If relevant, reasons for downgrading or nullifying or amending an ICSR
          should be included in the case narrative

       379.      The narrative should include the assessment of expectedness of each
          SUSAR by the sponsor including the grounds for expectedness that is if the event
          is not listed in RSI or if the severity/seriousness has increased. Any relevant
          autopsy or post-mortem ﬁndings should also be summarised.


7.30 Question: How should SUSARs of
   combination IMPs be reported?
       380.      Answer: When the treatment of a CT subject includes a combination of
          IMPs, the investigator should assess for every SAR if any of the IMPs could have
          caused it on the basis of medical judgement and without discarding causality for
          one IMP by only the fact that the suspected AR has been previously described for
          other IMP in the combination treatment.

18
     GVP Module VI Addendum II – Masking of personal data in ICSRs for EudraVigilance

                                                    24
     381.      Where the causality indicated by the investigator is suspected for several
        IMPs, the sponsor should assess the expectedness of the SAR considering the
        RSIs of all suspected IMPs when separate RSIs for each IMP are used (see
        Question 7.18). If the AR is unexpected for at least one of the IMPs (according to
        the separate RSIs), the SAR should be considered unexpected and reported as a
        SUSAR.

     382.         Where RSIs of the combination IMP in the IB or SmPC is used (see Question
        7.18), if a suspected SAR is not present in the RSI, it should be reported as a
        SUSAR. These SUSARs should be reported as related to the combination, unless
        it is – in rare cases – known to which IMP the SAR is related to.



     7.31 Question: is the risk proportionate safety
     recording and reporting possible in clinical
     trials ? What adverse event reporting should
     be performed in low intervention trials?
     383.       Answer: Safety recording and reporting in all clinical trials including low
        intervention trials can be risk proportionately adapted to the speciﬁcs of the
        clinical trial design and purpose. This must be speciﬁed and thoroughly justiﬁed
        in the respective protocol (CTR Art 41). It is expected that such justiﬁcation is
        supported by the risk assessment of the trial. For further guidance on the speciﬁc
        requirements, risk assessment and how to implement risk-adapted adverse event
        management in a clinical trial please see the respective recommendation paper
        on risk proportionate approaches in clinical trials19 as well as ICH E6 R320. The
        Sponsor should be aware that risk-based adaptation of adverse event
        management in a clinical trial protocol should not conﬂict with ICH E19 on a
        selective approach to safety data collection in speciﬁc late-stage pre-approval or
        post-approval clinical trials21 .


     7.32 Question: Should SUSARs or ARSs be
     submitted also to ethics committees?
     384.      Answer: Article 42 (SUSARs) and article 43 (ASRs) of the CTR1 describe the
        submission to the MSs (= NCA and Ethics Committee) through the electronic
        database for Safety reporting (EudraVigilance for SUSARs, and CTIS for ASRs).
        Additional direct submissions from sponsors to ethics committees are not
        foreseen.


19
   Risk proportionate approaches in clinical trials
20
   ICH E6(R3)
21
   ICH guideline E19 Step 5 on optimisation of safety data collection

                                                    25
385.     Ethics Committees can be involved in the assessment of safety
   information by the MSs, if that is the national decision of the individual MS.




7.33 Question: Should sponsors also send
SUSARs or safety ﬁndings to investigators of a
CT?
386.       Answer: The sponsor should promptly notify all concerned
   investigators/institutions of ﬁndings that could adversely aﬀect the safety of the
   subjects. New data that may aﬀect the subject’s safety, the beneﬁt-risk balance
   of the trial or the willingness of subjects to continue in the clinical trial should be
   communicated to subjects and investigators in a timely manner (ICH E6 (R3),
   section                                                                         3.13.1).
   The reporting of SUSARs to investigators/institutions should be in a manner that
   reﬂects the urgency of action required and should take into consideration the
   evolving knowledge of the safety proﬁle of the product (ICH E6 (R3) section
   3.13.2). Investigators should get informed of safety ﬁndings other than SUSARs
   that could aﬀect the safety of the subjects accordingly.

387.        SUSAR reporting to investigators is not mentioned in the CTR, however, it is
   of importance to inform investigators of changes to the safety proﬁle, but not
   individual SUSAR reports. The safety information for investigators should be
   concise and practical. When possible, information on SUSARs should contain a
   list of relevant blinded SUSARs, together with a summary analysis of the updated
   safety proﬁle, Risk Minimisation Measures, if applicable, and an updated
   beneﬁt/risk evaluation for the ongoing CTs. The frequency of such periodic reports
   to the investigators should be based on the nature of the research or clinical
   development project, the volume of SUSARs generated, on the emerged issue(s)
   and especially if the safety proﬁle changes.

388.      SUSAR reports contain unblinded data that usually should not be sent to
   investigators. The submission of individual safety reports to investigators may be
   justiﬁed if unblinded data is relevant for the management/treatment of a serious
   adverse reaction (SAR).

389.      In case of urgency and/or an impact on the beneﬁt- risk the Dear
   Investigator Letter might be part of a risk mitigation measure and therefore qualify
   as notiﬁcation of an urgent safety measure or an unexpected event impacting
   beneﬁt-risk balance of the subjects. These notiﬁcations should be followed by a
   substantial modiﬁcation when applicable, e.g. change of protocol. In case of
   information which is considered to have no/low impact on the safety of subjects,
   the submission can be done with the (next) substantial modiﬁcation.



                                          26
7.34 Question: When do requirements to
record and report safety issues start and end
for the investigator and the sponsor?
390.       AEs, including SAEs, should be recorded by the investigator from the signature of
   informed consent to the end of the trial unless otherwise provided for in the
   protocol, e.g. if AE/SAE occur in subjects before investigational product
   administration they should only be considered and reported to the sponsor if
   required by the protocol.
391.       SARs or follow-up information for a SAR that the investigator becomes
   aware of after the end of the trial should be reported to the sponsor (CTR Art 41
   and Annex III).
392.       The sponsor shall report all SUSARs from the beginning (see Question 10.2)
   to the end of the trial (see Question 10.12) and after the trial (CTR Art 42c), within
   timelines deﬁned in Article 42 and Annex III of CTR.
393.       While SAEs prior treatment often do not qualify as a SUSAR, these
   unfavourable medical events (ICH E6 (R3) may need to be notiﬁed to MSs e.g. as
   Unexpected Event (see Question 7.25 and 7.27).
394.       Reporting after end of CT depends on the speciﬁc characteristics / proﬁle,
   of the IMPs, like pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), toxicity and
   population of the CT and should be speciﬁed in the protocol. Standard operating
   procedures should be followed to ensure compliance with the necessary quality
   standards at every stage of case documentation, data collection, validation,
   evaluation, archiving, reporting and follow-up.




                                          27
      7.35 Question: How should pregnancy
      during the trial, medication errors, use
      outside the protocol, including misuse or
      abuse of IMPs be reported?
       395.       Answer: All reports of exposure during pregnancy (of subject or the
          partner), medication errors, use outside the protocol, including misuse or abuse
          in relation to the IMP should be recorded by the investigator and notiﬁed to the
          sponsor. If the medication error, pregnancy, misuse or abuse resulted in a SAE
          which was deemed related and unexpected in accordance with the RSI, it should
          be reported as a SUSAR. The general rules of the CTR as well as the guidance given
          in this Q&A document apply with regard to the expedited reporting of SUSARs
          (including reporting only unexpected SARs) in case of adverse events/reactions,
          the submission of ASR and the implementation of risk minimisation measures. If
          the (collected) medication error, pregnancy, misuse or abuse did not result in an
          AE, it should still be reported to the sponsor by the investigator (CTR Annex III
          section 2.1 number 2). The sponsor should reﬂect on and put corrective measures
          in place to prevent these in the future.


7d ANNUAL SAFETY REPORTS



7.36 Question: What should be the content and format
    of ASRs?
       396.       Answer: The main objective of ASRs is to present a comprehensive,
          thoughtful annual review and evaluation of pertinent safety information collected
          during the reporting period related to an IMP, whether or not it is marketed, by: (1)
          examining whether the information obtained by the sponsor during the reporting
          period is in accordance with previous knowledge of the IMP’s safety; (2) describing
          new safety issues that could have an impact on the protection of clinical trial
          subjects; (3) summarising the current understanding and management of
          identiﬁed and potential risks; and (4) providing an update on the status of the
          clinical investigation/development programme and study results22.




22
     ICH guideline E2F on development safety update report, Section 1.2.

                                                     28
       397.       ASRs should be concise and provide information to assure regulators that
          sponsors are adequately monitoring and evaluating the evolving safety proﬁle of
          the IMP. This includes also a description of the risk minimisation measures23. All
          safety issues discovered during the reporting period should be discussed in the
          text of the ASR; however, it should not be used to provide the initial notiﬁcation of
          signiﬁcant new safety information or provide the means by which new safety
          issues are detected22.
       398.       The content and format of an ASR should comply with ICH guideline E2F
          on Development Safety Update Report24 and CTR annex III section 3. Additional
          details are provided in dedicated questions:
                  • Question 7.37 regarding data protection,
                   •   Question 7.39 regarding multiple active substances,
                   •   Question 7.43 regarding reduced content of ASRs,
                   •   Questions 7.47 and 7.48 regarding EU/EEA-speciﬁc information.
       399.        ASRs should be written in English, irrespective of the MSCs.


7.37 Question: How to comply with CTR article 43
    section 3?
       400.      Answer: To comply with CTR article 43 section 3, stipulating that ASRs
          shall only contain aggregate and anonymised data, line listings should contain the
          information described in ICH guideline E2F section 3.7.2., except for the subject
          identiﬁcation code, as this information is only pseudonymised but not
          anonymised.

       401.      Instead, individual cases should be identiﬁed by the Worldwide Unique
          Case Identiﬁcation Number.

       402.       If no Worldwide Unique Case Identiﬁcation Number has been assigned,
          this unavailability should be indicated, but the subject identiﬁcation code should
          still not be provided.

       403.      If a sponsor is requested to provide further information on a certain case,
          the sponsor should be able to provide this information without revealing the
          subject identiﬁcation code and thus rendering the provided data as anonymous
          to the member states.




23
     ICH guideline E2F on development safety update report, Appendix C
24
     ICH guideline E2F on development safety update report

                                                    29
7.38 Question: When and for how long should sponsors
    submit ASRs?
  404.       Answer: ASRs should be submitted to CTIS from the ﬁrst authorisation of
     a clinical trial in any EU/EEA member state until the end of the last clinical trial
     conducted by the sponsor with the IMP in any EU/EEA member state. In cases
     where all clinical trials with the IMP have ended in all EU/EEA member states prior
     to the submission deadline of the ASR (i.e. 60 calendar days after the DLP), the
     submission of ASRs is not required1. Similarly, clinical trials that have ended (for
     the deﬁnition of the end of trial, reference should be made to Article 2(2)(26) of
     CTR) in all EU/EEA member states should not be linked in the submission of ASRs
     for ongoing clinical trials. The sponsor remains responsible for the ongoing safety
     evaluation of the investigational product(s) and for the managing of risks even
     after the end of the obligation to submit an ASR.

  405.      Submission of ASRs is not required in case the sponsor is conducting only
     a single trial with an IMP with a duration of less than one year.

  406.      Sponsors also need to submit ASRs for IMPs investigated in phase IV trials,
     low intervention trials and long-term follow-up trials.

  407.       ASRs should be submitted yearly within 60 days after the DLP24.

  408.       When subjects from diﬀerent clinical trials with various IMPs are being
     rolled over to long-term follow-up, for example in gene therapy trials, and the
     clinical development for the IMP is ongoing in the EU/EEA, the safety data of this
     IMP in all clinical trials, including safety data related to this IMP in the long-term
     follow-up study, should be covered within the ASRs of this IMP. If no clinical trials
     are ongoing with the respective IMP, the ASRs can be trial-speciﬁc for this one
     long-term follow-up clinical trial, covering safety data of all IMPs used or followed
     up, where no other clinical trial is ongoing.


7.39 Question: How should an ASR for combination
    including multidrug therapies be submitted?
  409.     Answer: In general, separate ASRs should be prepared for each active
     substance of a multi-drug therapy.




                                           30
  410.      Notwithstanding the general rule, a single ASR should be prepared for ﬁxed
     combination products, i.e. for products consisting of at least two active
     substances in a ﬁxed dose that are administered in a single dosage form (see CTR
     and Art. 43 and ICH E2F section 2.5). This approach can also be followed for multi-
     drug combinations where it is intended to develop a ﬁxed combination product. If
     the sponsor is also conducting clinical trials with individual component(s) of the
     ﬁxed combination product, separate ASR should be submitted for each
     component, and relevant ﬁndings from each ASR should be summarised in
     section 8.5 of the other ASR(s).

  411.        Notwithstanding the general rule, a single ASR may be prepared for trials
     involving multi-drug therapy, i.e. combinations of drugs that are not ﬁxed and not
     intended to be developed as a ﬁxed combination product (ICH E2F section 2.5)24.
     It is assumed that this approach is generally only applicable to trial-speciﬁc ASRs
     prepared by non-commercial sponsors.


7.40 Question: What is the Development International
    Birth Date, how is it deﬁned, and what is it used for?
  412.       Answer: The DIBD is used to determine the start of the annual period for
     the ASR. This date is the date of the sponsor’s ﬁrst authorisation to conduct the
     ﬁrst clinical trial with the IMP in any country worldwide (ICH E2F section 2.2).

  413.       The start of the annual period for the ASR is the month and date of the DIBD
     (e.g. when the DIBD is December 6th, each ASR period should cover the period
     from December 6th to December 5th of the following year). When the sponsor’s ﬁrst
     clinical trial is conducted in a country without a formal authorisation process, the
     sponsor should designate an appropriate date linked to the commencement of
     the ﬁrst clinical trial (ICH E2F section 2.2).

  414.      To aid harmonisation, it is strongly recommended that the DIBD is
     indicated by the sponsor within the ASR (ICH E2F section 3.1).

  415.       The data lock point (DLP) of an ASR should be the last day of the one-year
     reporting period. If desired by the sponsor, the DLP can be designated as the last
     day of the month prior to the month of the DIBD (e.g. when the DIBD is December
     6th, the DLP could be set to November 30th of the following year). ASRs should be
     submitted within 60 days after their DLP (ICH E2F section 2.2).




                                          31
7.41 Question: Can the DLP of an ASR be aligned with
    the DLP of the PSUR/PBRER?
     416.      Answer: When clinical development of a medicinal product continues
        following a marketing approval in any country worldwide, Periodic Safety Update
        Reports (PSURs), Periodic Beneﬁt-Risk Evaluation Reports (PBRERs) and ASRs
        should be submitted as speciﬁed by national or regional laws or regulations (ICH
        E2F section 2.2).

     417.      If desired by the sponsor, an ASR can be prepared based on the PSUR
        International Birth Date (IBD) so that the ASR and the PSUR can be synchronised
        (ICH E2F section 2.2).

     418.     In synchronising the data lock points for the ASR and PSUR, the period
        covered by the next ASR should be no longer than one year (ICH E2F section 2.2).

     419.       The data lock points for PSURs are available on the EMA website (Excel ﬁle
        “List of European Union reference dates (EURD) and frequency of submission of
        periodic safety update reports (PSURs)”, column E “DLP”)25.


7.42 Question: What date should be the start date and
    the end date of the ASR reporting period for
    investigator-initiated/academic clinical trials (not by
    the MAH (marketing authorisation holder))?
     420.      Answer: Where an ASR is submitted for one clinical trial, the start date of
        the ASR reporting period should be the DIBD, which is the date of the ﬁrst
        authorisation of this speciﬁc clinical trial. Alternatively, the sponsor may follow
        the approach described in question 7.41.

     421.      The end date of the ASR reporting period should be the DLP which is the
        day before the start of the reporting period i.e. when the start date of the reporting
        period is December 6th, the DLP is December 5th of the next year.

     422.       None of the ASR reporting periods should be longer than one year.




25
  Available at List of European Union reference dates (EURD) and frequency of submission of periodic
safety update reports (PSURs).

                                                  32
7.43 Question: Is a full ICH guideline E2F-compliant
    ASR always required? When could a simpliﬁed ASR
    be submitted?
       423.        Answer: The content of an ASR may be simpliﬁed in the following cases:

       424.      The ASR is prepared by a non-commercial sponsor for a single clinical trial,
          where the IMPs are authorised (for the deﬁnition of authorised investigational
          medicinal products, please refer to CTR article 2 paragraph 2 number 9) and where
          section 4.8 of the SmPC is used as RSI (for further information, please refer to CTR
          annex I section E number 28). Detailed instructions on what information is
          expected and what may be omitted in the above cases are available on the CTCG
          website26.

       425.       The ASR is prepared by a non-commercial sponsor for one or more clinical
          trials, and none of the trials has started yet (for the deﬁnition of the start of a
          clinical trial, please refer to CTR article 2 paragraph 2 number 25), or all clinical
          trials have been halted or suspended for more than one year without
          administration of the relevant investigational medicinal product(s) (for the
          deﬁnition of temporary halt and suspension of a clinical trial, please refer to CTR
          article 2 paragraph 2 numbers 27 and 28). In this case, a document stating that the
          trials have not started yet or have been halted or suspended for more than one
          year without administration of the investigational medicinal product(s), providing
          the results of the literature review (ICH guideline E2F section 3.13)24, providing the
          results of the IB/SmPC review (CTR article 55 paragraph 2, ICH guideline E2F
          section 3.4) and providing a statement on the beneﬁt-risk ratio of the trial and the
          necessity to update the protocol or the subject information sheet/ informed
          consent form (ICH guideline E2F section 3.20 is suﬀicient.

       426.       In all other cases, including cases where the above criteria are only
          partially met, a full ICH guideline E2F-compliant ASR should be submitted.




26
     CTCG Key documents list: Guidance, clinical trial safety, simpliﬁed template of Annual Safety Report.

                                                      33
7.44 Question: When a non-commercial sponsor runs
    several clinical trials with the same IMP or if
    diﬀerent non-commercial sponsors run
    independent clinical trials with the same non-
    authorised IMP, is one consolidated ASR needed?
  427.       Answer: For IMPs without a MA and where the clinical trial is supported by
     the developer, it is recommended that the developing company writes a single
     ASR per IMP covering all the safety information from the non-commercial clinical
     trials. See also ICH E2F section 2.4.2. This implies that SARs line listings,
     cumulative summary tabulation of SAEs, and the region-speciﬁc information
     which includes the cumulative summary tabulation of SARs, and list of patients
     who died or dropped out during the clinical trial should include also the data from
     the non-commercial sponsors. The ASR should clearly specify which data is
     included and from which clinical trials it originates, including the EU CT number.
     Submission of one single ASR on the IMP level is highly recommended if the same
     IMP (IMP combination) is used in several CTs. However, the member states
     concerned accept a trial-speciﬁc ASR if justiﬁed.

  428.       The submission of an ASR on the clinical trial level is encouraged in case
     the non-commercial sponsor uses several IMPs within the clinical trial where not
     all of them have support from the MAH, as thus safety information from those
     without support would not be incorporated into any ASR.


7.45 Question: Are ASRs required for placebos, active
    comparators and AxMPs?
  429.      Answer: ASRs are required for all IMPs other than placebo (CTR article 43
     paragraph 1), whereas IMPs are all medicinal products being tested or used as
     reference/ comparator (CTR article 2 paragraph 2 number 5).

  430.      Separate ASRs are not required for comparators, but relevant safety
     information should be included in the appropriate sections of the ASRs for the test
     investigational medicinal product (ICH guideline E2F section 1.3, among others).

  431.      ASRs are not required for AxMPs, but relevant safety information and any
     other safety issues should be included in the appropriate sections of the ASRs for
     the test IMP.




                                          34
7.46 Question: What information is required in the
    Cumulative Summary Tabulations of SAEs?
   432.       Answer: To enhance the utility of section 7.3 of the ASR, titled ‘Cumulative
      Summary Tabulations of Serious Adverse Events’ and in addition to the
      requirements speciﬁed in ICH guideline E2F, this section should also include the
      absolute numbers of patients treated as per the column headings, of the
      Cumulative Tabulation of SAEs. This information can be provided either in the text
      of the ASR or, preferably, directly within the table itself (see table below, adapted
      from table 6 of the ICH E2F guideline).


Cumulative summary tabulation of SAEs (example)




   433.     If feasible/possible the sponsor should also calculate patient-years of
      treatment. This information may be especially useful in the interpretation of data
      when there are substantial diﬀerences in time of exposure between subjects
      randomised to the tested product(s) and comparator(s).

   434.       A single Cumulative Summary Tabulation of SAEs should be presented for
      all clinical trials covered in the ASR. A sponsor may also include additional
      Cumulative Summary Tabulations of SAEs presented for separate populations or
      indications; however, these must be in addition to the single table covering all
      trials.

   435.       In a combined study, information related to SAEs occurring with the IVD or
      the IMD can be reported. For further details on IVD or MD please see “COMBINE
      Safety Reporting Sponsor Guide” and Q7.52 .



                                           35
7.47 Question: What ‘Region-Speciﬁc Information’ is
    required in the ASR in the EU/EEA?
       436.     Answer: The following EU/EEA-speciﬁc information is required in
          accordance with ICH guideline E2F section 3.16:

       •   Cumulative summary tabulation of SARs: The format should be the same as for
           the cumulative summary tabulation of SAEs (ICH E2F section 3.16 and table 6)
           and Question 7.46.
       •   List of subjects who died during the reporting period: The listing should include
           information on case number, assigned treatment (could still be blinded), causality
           to the study drug, and cause of death.

       437.       List of subjects who dropped out of clinical trials in association with an
          adverse event: The listing should include information on assigned treatment
          (could still be blinded), causality to the study drug, and cause of drop-out, i.e. the
          PT of the AE triggering the drop-out.

       •   Safety signals: The outcome of the safety signal review process during the ASR
           reporting period should be outlined. Potential new safety signals that were
           identiﬁed should be listed including a brief description of the signal, the date when
           the sponsor became aware of the signal, the status of the signal at the end of the
           reporting interval (closed or ongoing), the date when the signal was closed, if
           applicable, the source of the signal, a brief summary of the key data, plans for
           further evaluation and actions taken (i.e. proposed risk mitigation strategies). The
           outcome of the safety review should be provided in a tabular format. An example
           of such a table is presented below (Table 5 and Appendix C of ICH E2C (R2)) 27.
                Table format example for the outcome of the safety review in the ASR.




       438.     It is acknowledged that signal evaluation for clinical trials may not always
          be possible or appropriate, in which case a justiﬁcation for not including this
          information should be provided instead.


27
     ICH E2C (R2) Periodic beneﬁt-risk evaluation report - Scientiﬁc guideline.

                                                       36
  439.      The term ‘region-speciﬁc’ indicates that the above information is required
     in the EU/EEA, but not that only data collected in the EU/EEA should be
     considered.




7.48 Question: What RSI should be used for the ASR?
  440.      Answer: The RSI in eﬀect at the start of the reporting period shall serve as
     RSI during the reporting period.

  441.       For the purposes of ASRs, the RSI prepared on the basis of the data
     available at the DLP of the previous ASR may be considered the RSI in eﬀect at the
     start of the reporting period even if it was formally approved after the start of the
     reporting period.



7.49 Question: What should a sponsor be aware of
    during and after ASR submission to CTIS?
  442.      Sponsors are asked to check that the active substance(s) are completed in
     the structured ﬁelds when submitting an ASR in CTIS. Note that only the active
     substances for which the ASR is submitted should be ticked.

  443.       An ASR document submitted cannot be changed or withdrawn. In case
     there is a critical mistake or correction to be done, please check with the national
     contact point of the assigned Safet Assessing Member State (saMS) of this ASR
     (after the saMS selection has been completed). During an RFI process, an updated
     version of the ASR document can be uploaded.

  444.     Sponsors should be aware that the RFI on the ASR does not trigger any
     separate notice or alert in CTIS. One needs to actively monitor the ASR module.

  445.      Sponsors should be aware that the RFI on the so-called ad-hoc workﬂow
     does not trigger any separate notice or alert in CTIS. One needs to actively monitor
     the separate RFI tab for incoming RFIs on surveillance issues. These RFIs can be
     sent anytime and are not linked to any other application.

  446.      Sponsors should adhere to the deadlines given in the RFI raised within an
     ASR or ad-hoc workﬂow. In case a sponsor cannot meet the deadline, the national
     contact point of the MS raising the RFI should be contacted to discuss submitting
     the response after the deadline.




                                          37
   447.      In cases where a single ASR is prepared for a high number of clinical trials
      and/or a high number of investigational medical products must be selected for
      submission, or for clinical trials with diﬀerent sponsors, co-sponsors or CROs, the
      submitter may technically not be able to select all clinical trials covered by the
      ASR. In such case, multiple ASR submissions of the same ASR should be avoided,
      and the submitter is recommended to submit only one ASR to CTIS and select as
      many CTs covered by the ASR as possible: minimum should be the CT with the
      lowest EU CT number and the one with the highest EU CT number. The cover letter
      should list all CTs covered by the ASR and all member states concerned with the
      ASR. In addition, the co-sponsor (with equal responsibilities to safety surveillance
      and submission of the ASR) or the sponsor with diﬀerent Org ID of ‘the same
      sponsor’, or the diﬀerent sponsor (like non-commercial, where safety of the CT is
      covered within the developer’s ASR, see Question 7.43) should submit a
      document as ‘ASR’ in which they refer to the ASR submission and the ASR
      submission ID of the co-sponsor or other organization ID.
Note: This recommendation is valid till the technical limitation in CTIS has been solved.
   448.      For information, if applicable, an invoice for ASR assessment may be sent
      by MSCs and/or by the saMS, the latter may not be a MSC (nor the member state
      named in CTIS as saMS). The reason for this is that the responsibility of a saMS is
      per active substance, regardless of whether a saMS is an MSC in a clinical trial
      (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/20 article 2 section 2 letter c).


7.50 Question: Are there additional reporting
    requirements related to safety reporting under
    Chapter VII of the CTR to the member states, such
    as the submission of monthly, quarterly or half-
    yearly safety reports or SUSAR line listings?
   449.        Answer: Documents covering shorter than annual reporting periods, such
      as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly safety reports or SUSAR line listings, should
      only be submitted upon exceptional request by the RMS or the saMS for a clinical
      trial or IMP, respectively.

   450.      If they are requested, the sponsor will receive an RFI in the ad-hoc workﬂow
      to be able to submit the requested documents.




                                           38
7.51 Question: How long does the ASR assessment
    process last?
       451.      The assessment shall be completed within 42 days or in the case of an RFI
          within 84 days after the submission of the ASR28. This includes the time that
          sponsors have to respond to an RFI, which is usually 14 days. In practice,
          procedures may last longer than 84 days due to several reasons, including
          multiple RFIs.


7.52 Question: What information is required in the ASR
    in case of combined studies?
       452.      The Annual Safety Report should summarize the relevance of information
          concerning SAEs related to investigational medical devices (IMDs) or
          investigational in vitro diagnostic medical devices (IIVDs) and device deﬁciencies
          (DDs) that theoretically could lead to SAEs observed during the reporting period in
          the “evaluation of risks” section or where appropriate in the section “beneﬁt-risk
          considerations”. For more guidance also view “COMBINE Safety Reporting
          Sponsor Guide” [Reference will be added when available].

       453.      If actions for safety reasons have been taken during the ASR reporting
          period due to SAEs related to investigational medical devices (IMDs) or
          investigational in vitro diagnostic medical devices (IIVDs), this should also be
          mentioned in the appropriate section of the ASR.



7.53 Question: The Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No
    536/2014 mentions only some aspects speciﬁc to
    radiopharmaceuticals, it does not specify any
    documentation regarding exposure to ionising
    radiation in clinical trials. Does that mean that
    sponsors are no longer expected to present such
    information in the protocol and/or application?
       454.       Answer: No, the sponsor is expected to include information on exposure
          to ionising radiation in the protocol in line with CTR Annex I, section D to allow



28
     Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/20; article 7 paragraph 1 letter c.

                                                     39
          assessment of the beneﬁts and risks of the clinical trial, see CTR article 6
          paragraph 1 (b)(i) and (ii).
       455.       The speciﬁcs of the information to be included will depend on the situation
          of exposure (see below).
       456.       Exposure to ionising radiation in clinical trials can be divided into two main
          situations – radiodiagnostic procedures and radiotherapeutic procedures.

       •   Radiodiagnostic procedures include both radiological procedures and nuclear
           medicine procedures. In the diagnostic situation, the ionising radiation exposure
           is a consequence of the procedure, and the risk to the trial participants therefore
           needs to be justiﬁed in the clinical trial protocol. The ALARA principle prevails, i.e.,
           the exposure should be maintained as low as reasonably achievable without
           compromising the diagnostic imaging quality. In line with ICRP 29 criteria and CTR
           article 6, paragraph 1(b)(ii)) the risks and inconveniences for the trial subjects
           regarding interventions involving radiation exposure should be justiﬁed in
           comparison to the exposure involved in the procedures used in normal clinical
           practice. When discussing the beneﬁts and risks in the protocol, sponsors should
           describe the following in order to provide maximum clarity minimising then
           number of Request For Information (RFI) considerations based on lack of
           information, possibly in a protocol appendix if Member State-diﬀerences in
           national Standard of Care are envisaged: risk category of trial participants
           according to criteria, radiodiagnostic trial procedures, maximum eﬀective dose
           per procedure (mSv), number of procedures/trial participant/year, and estimated
           number of additional radiodiagnostic procedures/trial participant/year compared
           to normal clinical practice for the same indication.

       •   Radiotherapeutic procedures can be further divided into external beam
           radiotherapy, brachy therapy and systemic radiation therapies with
           radiopharmaceuticals. Only the latter is subject to regulation by the CTR. With
           therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals, the radiation dose absorbed by tissues and
           organs is the mechanism of action through which eﬀicacy of the therapy is
           achieved, but it may also cause toxicity. The risks of both ineﬀective treatment due
           to insuﬀicient absorbed dose to the target lesions and risks of severe/irreversible
           long-term toxicity due to excessive absorbed dose to risk organs, need to be
           monitored and mitigated during the trial to optimise the beneﬁts and risks for the
           individual trial participant, in line with article 6.1(b)(i) and (ii) of the CTR. The
           AHASA principle prevails – the absorbed radiation dose to the target tissue(s)
           should be as high as safely attainable, i.e., preventing severe and/or irreversible
           long- term toxicity while at the same time maintaining a high likelihood of eﬀicacy.
           In addition to the beneﬁt/risk section, sponsors should describe dosimetric
           procedures in the protocol, as well as target absorbed doses (in Gy) to tumour
           lesions and dose limits to risk organs based on the best available evidence as well

29
     ICRP, 1992. Radiological Protection in Biomedical Research. ICRP Publication 62. Ann. ICRP 22 (3)

                                                      40
   as any necessary adaptations of the treatment plan e.g. due to combination
   therapy that may aﬀect the biological eﬀect of the radiation therapy.

457.     In order to assess the beneﬁts and risks, any deviations from the principles
   above should be justiﬁed in the protocol.




                                       41
         AUTHORISATION OF MANUFACTURING AND
                 IMPORTATION OF IMPS

8.1. Question: A clinical trial with an
investigational medicinal product (IMP) which is
an oﬀicinal or magistral formula falls within the
scope of the Clinical Trials Regulation. What
does this mean for the requirements as regards
manufacturing authorisation?
458. Answer: Chapter IX of the Clinical Trials Regulation applies to the
     manufacturing and import of the investigational medicinal product
     (IMP), which is subject to the holding of an authorisation. However,
     article 61 (5) of the Regulation provides for exceptions where an
     authorisation is not required under certain conditions. The conditions
     to beneﬁt for these exemptions are that the IMPs having undergone one
     of the processes referred to in Article 61(5)(a), (b) and (c)1 shall be used
     for the same clinical trial for which the process was done, the IMPs
     should be used in the same Member State where the process was
     done, or in an other Member State in which the same trial is being
     conducted and if this Member State allows it, but the IMPs are not
     necessarily used in the same hospitals, health centres or clinics where
     the preparation of the IMP was done.
459. The preparation of investigational medicinal products with an oﬀicinal
     or magistral formula does not require a manufacturing authorisation
     where this process is carried out in hospitals, health centres or clinics for
     exclusive use in these same places taking part in the same clinical trial
     in the same Member State.
460. In such cases Member States shall set up appropriate and
     proportionate requirements, including regular inspections, to ensure
     subject safety and reliability and robustness of the data generated in
     the clinical trial.




1
 re-labelling or repackaging, preparation of radiopharmaceuticals used as diagnostic investigational
medicinal products and preparation of medicinal products referred to in points (1) and (2) of Article 3
of Directive 2001/83/EC for use as investigational medicinal products)


                                                           1
8.2. Question: What are the regulatory
requirements for the preparation and labelling of
radiopharmaceuticals used as diagnostic
investigational medicinal products?
461. Answer: the preparation of radiopharmaceuticals used as diagnostic
     investigational medicinal products do not require a manufacturing
     authorisation where this process is carried out in hospitals, health
     centres or clinics for exclusive use in these same places taking part in
     the same clinical trial in the same Member State2.
462. In line with article 68 of the CTR, radiopharmaceuticals used as IMP or
     AxMP do not need to adhere to the labelling requirements in article 66
     and 67. Nevertheless, the product must be labelled appropriately in
     order to ensure subject safety and reliability and robustness of the
     data generated.




8.3. Question: What documentation is
required in the application for the authorisation
of a clinical trial relating to compliance with
good manufacturing practice (GMP) for an
investigational medicinal product?
463. Answer: The documentation required to show compliance of the IMP and AxMP
     with GMP is outlined in Chapter IX and Annex 1 section F of the Clinical Trials
     Regulation:


       a) For IMPs authorised in the EU (even if not manufactured in the EU) no
          documentation is required.
       b) For IMPSs that are not authorised in the EU and do not have a marketing
          authorisation from a third country that is party to ICH, and are not manufactured
          in the EU, an authorisation referred to in article 61(1) and a QP declaration of GMP
          equivalence is required. In the latter case, if a Mutual recognition Agreement
          (MRA) covering also clinical trials is in place with the particular country, the latter
          declaration is not required if the MRA provides for GMP equivalence already.


2
    Article 61 (5) of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014

                                                    2
   c) In all other cases, an authorisation according to article 61 of the Clinical trial
      Regulation) is required.


Information regarding the GMP compliance of the active pharmaceutical ingredients is
not required by the CTR (and can therefore not be required by the Member States
Concerned.)




8.4. Question: Are there speciﬁc requirements for the
labelling of cryopreserved medicinal products?
464. Answer: CTR Annex VI labelling requirements should be fulﬁlled. However,
     considering the cryopreserved nature of certain IMPs (such as deep cryopreserved
     products) and the possible risks due to re-labelling, it may be proportionate to omit
     CT reference code and subject identiﬁcation number from the immediate
     packaging label, if adequately justiﬁed in the IMPDQ and label section or in the
     protocol. In these cases, information should be provided on how subject safety,
     traceability as well as reliability and robustness of the data generated in the clinical
     trial are ensured by other measures, e.g. by providing the respective information on
     secondary packaging or accompanying letter.

465. For ATMP, traceability should be veriﬁed in accordance with article 15 of Regulation
     (EC) No 1394/2007.

466. Digital stand-alone solutions (such as a QR-code only system) for primary
     packaging labels are not endorsed.




                                             3
               “INFORMED CONSENT” AND OTHER
                SUBSTANTIAL REQUIREMENTS FOR
                  CONDUCTING CLINICAL TRIALS


9.1. Question:       What    is   meant   by
‘compensation for participation’ in a trial
involving incapacitated subjects, minors and
pregnant and breast feeding women?
467. Answer: according to article 31(1)(d), article 32(1)(d) and article 33(d)
     of the Clinical Trials Regulation no incentives or ﬁnancial
     inducements, other than compensation for the participation in the
     clinical trial, are to be given to incapacitated subjects, legal
     representatives, minors and pregnant and breast feeding women. This
     compensation should not cover more than expenses and loss of
     earning, directly related to the participation in the clinical trials.
     Examples of expenses directly related to the participation in the
     clinical trials are travel costs for the participating subject and the
     legally designated representative (if applicable) or (if applicable) the
     person accompanying the subject, costs for accommodation, or
     additional costs due to participation in the clinical trial collected by
     the subjects’ health insurance (compulsory patient contributions/own
     risk). The information on compensation shall be submitted in the
     application dossier (CTR Annex I, P(70)) and as such is subject to
     assessment by Member States. A small token of appreciation is not
     considered an incentive, but needs to be explicitly allowed by the
     ethics committee.



9.2. Question: When can the obligation to
ensure the compensation of a damage of article
76 stop?
468. Answer: According to article 76 of the Clinical Trials Regulation, a
     clinical trial may be undertaken only if provision has been made for
     ensuring that a subject is compensated for any damage suﬀered
     which resulted from participation in a clinical trial. The sponsor shall

                                            1
      make use of any appropriate arrangements existing in the Member
      State concerned (be it an insurance or guarantee or a similar
      arrangement).

469. There are no speciﬁc Union provisions on when the obligation of
     providing compensation for damage suﬀered in a clinical trial should
     stop.
470. However, the purpose of article 76 of the Clinical Trials Regulation is
     to ensure that a clinical trial subject will obtain compensation for
     damages caused by participating in the clinical trial independently of
     the ﬁnancial capacity of the investigator/sponsor. Article 76 stresses
     also that any damage should be compensated. In view of this purpose
     of the provision the sponsor should ensure that the arrangements
     ensuring the compensation of damage are in place for the period in
     which such damages can arise and lawfully be claimed by the clinical
     trials subject.
471. The obligation to ensure the compensation of a damage proposed by
     the sponsor should be subject to assessment by each Member State
     according with national law.




9.3. Question: What is meant by “the
informed consent shall be documented” (article
29(1) of the Clinical Trials Regulation)?
472. Answer: Informed consent should be written, dated and signed by the
     person performing the interview and by the subject or the legally
     designated representative in cases when the subject is unable to give
     informed consent. Appropriate alternative means can be used to give
     and record informed consent in cases when the subject is unable to
     write. This should be done in the presence of at least one impartial
     witness. Details of the process shall be recorded and the informed
     consent form shall be kept as evidence.




                                           2
9.4. Question: What is meant by “his or her express
informed consent shall be obtained before the
subject can continue to participate in the Clinical
Trial” (article 32(3) of the Clinical Trials Regulation)?
   473. As soon as a minor participating in a clinical trial reaches the age of legal
        competence (as deﬁned in national law, which varies between 12 and 18
        years), he/she needs to express his/her informed consent to continuing
        participation in the study by signing the informed consent form, after having
        been properly informed, in line with the requirements of the Clinical Trials
        Regulation.

          For this purpose, the investigator should provide the trial subject with an
          information sheet and informed consent form appropriate for the age of
          legal competence. The information sheet and informed consent form may
          be provided prior to the trial subject's attainment of legal competence (e.g.
          during the last visit before reaching the age of legal competence), which
          would be an opportunity to clarify any questions. The interview that is
          required under Article 29(2)(c) of the Clinical Trials Regulation should take
          place once the trial subject has reached the age of legal competence. The
          new informed consent shall be in writing, dated and signed by the person
          performing the interview and by the trial subject in accordance with Article
          29(1) of the Clinical Trials Regulation (unless an exception as provided for in
          Article 29(1) applies or when the requirements listed under Article 30 are
          met). The information process and signature of the informed consent should
          take place before any further clinical trial protocol-related actions are
          taken, e.g., at the next study visit or, depending on the delay between the
          age of legal competence and the next visit, at a visit organised for this
          purpose, when practically feasible, without putting an undue burden on the
          trial subject. This process should not result in a treatment or care
          interruption, which would be detrimental to the trial subject.

          The procedure of obtaining the new written informed consent is
          independent of the medium chosen (paper-based or electronic) and it
          should be described in the trial protocol, the informed consent form and the
          information sheet (including maximum timelines accepted for the
          additional visit, if applicable) and shall be authorised by the Member States
          concerned (MSC).




                                                   3
9.5. Could the provisions in article 35 on
“deferred informed consent” be used when there
is not suﬀicient time to obtain informed consent,
even though the objective of the trial is not to
study a medical emergency situation?
474. Answer: No. The medical condition studied must be directly related to
     the emergency situation. There must always be a medically justiﬁed
     need to perform the ﬁrst intervention within a short time frame in
     relation to the emergency situation,


9.6. Is a trial with a mixed subject population,
where some subjects consent prior to inclusion
and others after the ﬁrst trial-speciﬁc
intervention, still an emergency trial?
475. Answer: Yes. Article 35 is applicable if the protocol provides for
     inclusion of any subjects without prior informed consent in a medical
     emergency. If prior informed consent is possible to obtain from some
     subjects (or their legal representatives) but not from others, the
     protocol should clearly explain the reasons and justiﬁcation for this
     mixed population. It should not be possible to perform the clinical trial
     as an emergency trial if informed consent can be obtained from ALL
     subjects or from his/her legally designated representative.


9.7. Is the use of placebo allowed in a clinical
trial in an emergency situation?
476. Answer: Only trials in emergency situations where scientiﬁc grounds
     exist to expect a potential for a direct clinically relevant beneﬁt for
     participating subjects as deﬁned in Article 35.1 (b) can be carried out.
     Where comparison is performed between one or several treatment
     arms receiving active treatment vs. a control arm, no subject should
     receive inferior treatment compared to normal clinical practice in a
     Member State, why placebo-treatment should be restricted to
     situations where it is added to such standard of care.




                                            4
9.8. What is meant by a subject’s prior
objection to participate in an emergency
situation trial?
477. Answer: If objections to trial participation can be identiﬁed among
     personal belongings of the subject or are known to the investigator
     responsible for subject inclusion, e.g. found to be clearly stated in the
     medical record, national registries (if available), such concerns
     should be respected.



9.9. When should informed consent be
sought in an emergency situation trial and what
happens to the data obtained if a subject dies
before informed consent has been given or if the
subject or his/her legally designated
representative does not agree to provide
informed consent?
478. Answer: Informed consent must be sought without undue delay and
     these eﬀorts must be duly documented in the medical record of the
     subject, e.g. clearly mentioned in the source documents of the
     recovery of the conscience and, where relevant, describing eﬀorts to
     reach a legal representative.

479. In situations when the subject dies before any informed consent has
     been provided, and the data already gathered has been collected in
     agreement with Article 35, the data should remain in the trial. In
     situations when the subject or his/her legally designated
     representative do not consent but instead disagree with continued
     trial participation, no further research data can be collected. The data
     already provided will be kept in the trial if all prerequisites in Article 35
     have been fulﬁlled, including that eﬀorts seeking informed consent
     have not been unduly delayed.




                                               5
9.10. Are secondary objectives and
corresponding endpoints acceptable even if
they are without any expected direct clinically
relevant beneﬁt for the subject but instead
could provide a group beneﬁt for patients?
480. Answer: The main objective of an emergency situation trial should
     always meet the legal requirement for a scientiﬁc basis for the potential
     to have a direct clinically relevant beneﬁt for the subject.

481. This would make it possible to gather pharmacokinetic and biomarker
     data, as long as such secondary or exploratory endpoints do not pose
     more than minimal risk and burden for subjects.
